newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan sets single China investment cap at $50 mln.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan sets single China investment cap at $50 mln.

text.p: Taiwan's economics ministry on Tuesday night told business executives that it has set a ceiling for single investments by local firms in China at US$50 million, several local newspapers reported on Wednesday.
A ministry spokesman contacted by Reuters declined to confirm all the details, but said the ministry may announce more information later in the day.
According to the new rules, the total investment for each firm listed in the main stock exchange or the over-the-counter stock exchange will vary according to their sizes, the papers said.
The ministry does not currently set ceilings on single investments in China but listed firms cannot invest more than 40 percent of their paid-in capital in China, he said.
According to the new rules, listed firms with net asset value under T$5 billion can invest up to 40 percent of their net asset value, the papers said.

Those with net asset value between T$5 billion and T$10 billion can invest up to 30 percent of their net asset value, and those with net asset value exceeding T$10 billion can invest as much as 20 percent of their net asset value, they said.
Unlisted firms, or any listed firms' shareholders using personal names to invest in China, can invest up to T$60 million in total investment, the papers said.
Taiwan has banned direct investment and trade with China since a civil war split them in 1949.

Since a political thaw began in the late 1980s, some 30,000 Taiwan firms have poured over US$30 billion into the mainland, making Taiwan one of China's top overseas investors and China one of Taiwan's most important markets.

Increased political and even military tensions since 1995 have prompted Taiwan's Nationalist government to call for more caution in mainland investing, warning that the island must not become overdependent on its adversary's economy.
Several major Taiwan firms have called off China projects in apparent compliance.
The ministry has been working on the new investment rules for months and has invited suggestions from economists and other experts on rules that could effectively control investment in rival China.
